If normalization is performed in the setter, it becomes impossible to input values directly. Serialization must be done using a vector that is not normalized, with normalization performed internally. This is the same as properties like the gravity direction in SpringBoneSimulator.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/00171519-54bc-45dd-af71-b41493cb3876

However, as mentioned above, if the static two-hole arc approach is used, this property will be deprecated altogether.

+<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
+<class name="JointLimitationKusudama3D" inherits="JointLimitation3D" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:noNamespaceSchemaLocation="../class.xsd">
+	<brief_description>
+		A Kusudama joint limitation that constrains bone orientation using multiple cones connected by tangent paths.
+	</brief_description>
+	<description>
+		JointLimitationKusudama3D represents a spherical constraint region using multiple sequence cones that are automatically connected by smooth tangent paths. The term "Kusudama" originates from Japanese papercraft models made by sewing or gluing pyramidal units through a common vertex, which this constraint visually resembles.
+		[b]How Kusudamas Work:[/b]
+		Each cone is defined by a center direction and a radius (radii may vary per cone). The constraint allows bone orientations within any of these cones. Additionally, adjacent cones in the sequence are automatically connected by tangent paths, creating a smooth transition region between cones. The inside of tangent circles is forbidden, while the region outside both tangent circles (between the cones) forms the allowed path.
+		[b]Important:[/b] Cones form a linear sequence, not a closed loop. The last cone in the array does not automatically connect back to the first cone. To create a closed constraint region, you must explicitly add a final cone that connects back to the first, or arrange your cones so the last one naturally connects to the first.
+		[b]Constraint Solving Process:[/b]
+		If there are no cones ([code]cone_count[/code] is 0), the constraint is effectively disabled and the bone direction is returned unchanged. Otherwise:
+		1. First, the solver checks if the bone direction is within any sequence cone. If so, the orientation is allowed.
+		2. If not, it checks if the bone direction is within the tangent path regions between adjacent cones.
+		3. If the bone is outside all allowed regions, it is constrained to the nearest boundary point.
+		The solver is [b]stateless[/b]: output depends only on the current input direction. When the input is [b]just outside[/b] a cone (within ~2° of its boundary), that cone's boundary point is returned for continuity. Otherwise boundaries are scored in [b]exponential map (expmap) space[/b] (tangent at the first cone center): [code]score = d_sq_expmap + k * chord_dist[/code]. The solver uses [b]smooth Voronoi power[/b] (e=2) for weights [code]w_i = 1/(score_i^2 + ε)[/code], then the [b]Karcher (Fréchet) mean[/b] on the sphere: start from the Euclidean weighted average normalized, then 8 geodesic gradient steps (log-map tangent sum, exp-map back) for minimal sum jerk. If the input is near antipodal to the first cone center, it falls back to [code]score = dot(boundary, input) - k * distance[/code]. [b]Discontinuities[/b]—output jumping between boundaries for small input change—are bugs.
+		[b]Use case:[/b] Typical 3-cone setups model joints like knees, elbows, and shoulders: bone direction is constrained to cones plus tangent paths. Knees and elbows often have [b]long-and-thin[/b] limitations (one cone with a larger radius for the main bend, two with smaller radii); shoulders tend to have a [b]weirder shape[/b] (less symmetric, more irregular cone layout). When posing, the direction sweeps through the allowed region; the Karcher mean over smooth Voronoi weights keeps output continuous at boundaries and minimizes jerk (flipping or snapping to the opposite side).
